questions.stem: What is the difference between a system being useful and being usable?
options: Useful means it is cheap; usable means it is expensive
Useful means it fulfils the business requirements; usable means how easy and automated it is for operational tasks
Useful means it is in the cloud; usable means it is on-premises
Useful means it is documented; usable means it is tested
questions.explanation: Useful means a system fulfils requirements and performs the operational tasks; usable means how easy and automated it is, making the operator's life easy.

questions.stem: In the marketing-campaign example, why is dumping data from five source systems into a Data Lake useful but not usable?
options: Because a Data Lake cannot store structured data
Because all the data is in one place but not yet in a format the marketing team can easily use for campaigns
Because the marketing team lacks access rights
Because the data has not been encrypted
Because five systems is too many
questions.explanation: Having all data centralised is useful, but it is not usable until converted into a format, such as a Data Warehouse, Data Mart or Semantic Layer, that the marketing team can readily use.

questions.stem: Where should data be formatted so that it becomes usable for the relevant team?
options: In a Data Warehouse, a Data Mart or a Semantic Layer
questions.explanation: Unless data is formatted in a Data Warehouse, Data Mart or Semantic Layer it may not be usable for the relevant team.

questions.stem: What proportion of data in the Big Data era is said to come from semi- and unstructured sources?
questions.explanation: In the current era 90% or more of data comes from semi- and unstructured sources, all of which is useful but not usable until structured.

questions.stem: Which standard's definition of usability is quoted: 'the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use'?
questions.explanation: The quoted definition of usability comes from the ISO 9241 standard.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the listed dimensions of Data Usability?
options: Data should be relevant for the stakeholders
Data Quality should be high so stakeholders can trust it
Enough data points should be available for decision making
Data should be stored on-premises only
Data should be available in an easy-to-use format for analysis
questions.explanation: Relevance, quality, sufficiency, accessibility and ease-of-use format are the dimensions; on-premises storage is not among them.

questions.stem: In the characteristics of Data Usability, what does 'Effective' mean?
questions.explanation: Effective is defined as accurate and impactful; Efficient is the characteristic that means time bound.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of Data Usability means data is easy to download or send to other systems?
questions.explanation: Utilisable is defined as easy to download or send to other systems.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of Data Usability refers to use on multiple types of devices such as desktops, laptops, mobiles and tablets?
questions.explanation: Reusable is the characteristic concerned with use on multiple device types, including desktops, laptops, mobiles and tablets.

questions.stem: What is the ideal action for semi- and unstructured data so that stakeholders can use it?
options: Leave it in its raw form in the Data Lake
Delete it once it has been viewed
Convert it into structured format inside a proper data model
questions.explanation: Ideally all semi- and unstructured data should be converted into structured format inside a proper data model for stakeholders, otherwise there is no point holding it.
